title: CORNER C6 Notes: The Ecosystem
summary: C6 forward-looking notes. White-label, multi-language, voice interface, Corner SDK, enterprise tier, third-party skill marketplace, API integrations, AI-to-AI collaboration, brand partnerships. Early thinking for the ecosystem layer.
content:
CORNER C6 Notes: The Ecosystem

Author: Steve (AI Advisory Lead) Date: 2026-03-16 Depends on: C5 complete (self-service signup, XP UI, furniture marketplace, skills gallery, neighbor offices, trend charts, ROI reports, push notifications, App Store listing) Status: Early thinking. Not a build spec yet. Becomes a full spec when C5 is halfway done.

What C5 Delivered

C5 made Corner sticky. Self-service signup with Stripe, XP/streaks/leaderboard, furniture marketplace, room editor, weekly recaps, trend charts, ROI reports, skills gallery, neighbor offices, push notifications, App Store listing. Clients sign up without AOM intervention, build a world they're invested in, and see data-backed proof of value every month.

C5 answered: "Why do they never leave?" Because leaving means losing their world.

C6 answers: "How does this become an ecosystem?"

C6 Is the Ecosystem Layer

C5 is one product for one type of customer (SMBs buying directly from AOM). C6 expands who sells Corner, who builds for Corner, who uses Corner, and how they interact with it. This is where Corner stops being a product and becomes a platform that other businesses build on top of.

The difference: C1-C5 revenue = AOM selling to clients. C6 revenue = other people selling Corner for AOM, building on Corner for AOM, and expanding Corner's market without AOM doing the work.

1. White-Label Corner

Concept

Agencies, consultants, and managed service providers resell Corner under their own brand. AOM powers the backend. The reseller handles sales, onboarding, and client relationships. Corner becomes invisible infrastructure.

Why This Matters

AOM's sales bottleneck is Patrik + Ash + Jacob doing outreach. White-label multiplies sales capacity by N where N = number of resellers. Each reseller brings their own client base, their own vertical expertise, their own sales team.

The math: if 10 resellers each bring 5 clients/month at $3k = $150k new MRR/month. AOM's cut at 60%: $90k/month. No sales effort from AOM.

Implementation Notes

White-label customization layers:

  • Brand: logo, colors, fonts, product name (their clients never see "Corner" or "AOM")
  • Domain: ai.theirbrand.com instead of corner.app
  • Email: transactional emails come from their domain
  • Onboarding: custom welcome messages, their company name in greetings
  • Support: their support email/chat, not AOM's

What stays the same (non-customizable):

  • Backend infrastructure (Docker containers, provisioning, updates)
  • Agent architecture (CC + relay + skills)
  • Skill library (they get all AOM premium skills)
  • Game engine (isometric rooms, modes, XP system)
  • Supabase schema and data layer

Reseller tiers:

Tier Monthly Min Revenue Share White-Label Clients
Partner $5k/mo 70/30 (reseller/AOM) No (Corner branded) Unlimited
Silver $15k/mo 65/35 Yes (their brand) Unlimited
Gold $30k/mo 60/40 Yes + custom onboarding Unlimited
Platinum $75k/mo 55/45 Yes + dedicated infrastructure Unlimited

Revenue share applies to the reseller's collected client fees. AOM's 30-45% covers infrastructure, updates, and platform maintenance.

Reseller dashboard (admin panel extension):

  • Reseller logs into admin.corner.app/reseller (or their white-label admin URL)
  • Sees only their clients (Supabase RLS on reseller_id)
  • Can provision new clients, manage existing, push skill updates to their fleet
  • Revenue dashboard: their client count, MRR, AOM's share, payout history
  • Cannot access other resellers' clients or AOM's direct clients

Technical requirements:

  • Supabase: resellers table (id, company_name, domain, brand_config, tier, revenue_share_pct)
  • Supabase: organizations.reseller_id FK (null for direct AOM clients)
  • Caddy: multi-domain routing (each reseller's domain resolves to the same server, brand config loaded per request)
  • Email: per-reseller sending domain (or AOM sends on their behalf with their reply-to)
  • Onboarding: brand config injected into the wizard (logo, colors, welcome text)
  • Container: reseller_id label on each container for fleet segmentation

Open questions:

  • Does the reseller set their own pricing (client pays reseller, reseller pays AOM)? Or does AOM set pricing and split?
    • Recommendation: reseller sets pricing. They know their market. AOM takes a flat % of whatever they charge.
  • Can resellers build custom skills for their clients?
    • Yes. Custom skills uploaded through the reseller dashboard, pushed to their fleet only. Not visible to other resellers or AOM direct clients.
  • Can a reseller's client switch to AOM direct (or another reseller)?
    • Yes, with 30-day notice. Data portable. But switching means losing the reseller's custom skills and brand. This is a natural retention tool for the reseller.

2. Multi-Language Support

Concept

Corner in Spanish, Japanese, German, French, Portuguese, Chinese (Simplified), Korean, Arabic. Expand TAM globally. The isometric game is visual and requires minimal translation. The text surfaces (HUD, settings, notifications, skill descriptions) need i18n.

Implementation Notes

What needs translation:

  • UI strings: HUD labels, button text, menu items, settings labels, error messages
  • Onboarding wizard: question text, placeholder text, progress labels
  • Agent names and descriptions (default set, client can rename in any language)
  • Skill descriptions and documentation
  • Notification messages (push + in-app)
  • Weekly recap text ("Your team is ready. Let's go." in 8 languages)
  • ROI report text and labels
  • Email templates

What does NOT need translation:

  • Agent conversation (CC already speaks every language natively)
  • Isometric sprites/art (visual, language-independent)
  • Furniture names (can be translated, but works in English as a universal default)
  • Code/technical layer

i18n framework:

  • next-intl or react-i18next (Bobby's call, both work with Next.js)
  • Translation files: JSON per language per namespace (en/common.json, es/common.json, en/onboarding.json, etc.)
  • Language detection: browser language > user setting > default (English)
  • Language switcher in Settings > Language (dropdown with flag icons)
  • URL structure: no language prefix (single domain, language stored in user profile). Alternative: corner.app/es/app if SEO for the marketing site matters.

Translation workflow:

  • Phase 1: English (done, it's the current language)
  • Phase 2: Spanish (largest non-English market in US, Phoenix is 40% Hispanic)
  • Phase 3: Japanese, German, French (tech-forward markets with AI adoption)
  • Phase 4: Portuguese, Chinese, Korean, Arabic (global expansion)

Translation source: Professional translation for UI strings (not machine translation for the product). Budget ~$2-5k per language for initial translation, ~$500/language/quarter for updates. Alternatively: use Anthropic's Claude to generate initial translations, then have native speakers review. Much cheaper.

RTL support: Arabic requires right-to-left layout. The isometric game is unaffected (visual). HUD, settings, and text surfaces need RTL CSS. This is non-trivial but doable with Tailwind's rtl: variant.

3. Voice Interface

Concept

Talk to your agents via voice. Walk into your isometric office, press a button (or use a hotword), speak your request, see the agent respond in their speech bubble AND hear the response via TTS.

Why This Is Powerful

Most AI chat is text. Voice changes the interaction model:

  • Contractor on a job site: hands dirty, can't type. Voice command: "Bobby, what's the status on the Smith project permit?"
  • CPA driving to a client: "Calendar, what do I have at 2 PM?"
  • Business owner walking: "Operations, send a follow-up to the Johnson lead."

Voice makes Corner usable in contexts where text-based AI tools can't compete. It's the difference between a dashboard you sit at and an assistant that's always with you.

Implementation Notes

Speech-to-Text (STT):

  • Web Speech API (free, built into Chrome/Safari, decent accuracy)
  • Alternatively: Whisper API (OpenAI, $0.006/min, higher accuracy, works offline via WASM)
  • Recommendation: Web Speech API for C6 launch (free, good enough). Whisper as premium upgrade.

Text-to-Speech (TTS):

  • ElevenLabs API: highest quality, multiple voices, ~$0.30/1k chars at Scale tier
  • Alternatively: Web Speech API (free, robotic but functional)
  • Recommendation: ElevenLabs for premium ("Your agents have a voice"), Web Speech API as free fallback

Agent voices (ElevenLabs):

  • Each agent type gets a distinct voice:
    • Operations: calm, professional male voice
    • Calendar: friendly, upbeat female voice
    • Email Triage: crisp, efficient neutral voice
    • Outreach: confident, warm male voice
    • Content: creative, energetic female voice
    • QA: precise, measured neutral voice
  • Clients can choose voice presets in Settings > Agents > [Agent] > Voice

Voice interaction flow:

  1. Client presses mic button in chat bar (or says hotword "Hey Corner" if enabled)
  2. Recording indicator appears (pulsing circle on chat bar)
  3. Client speaks their request
  4. Release mic button (or pause detection ends recording after 2s silence)
  5. STT converts audio to text
  6. Text appears in chat bar as a regular message (client can edit before sending)
  7. Message routes to the focused agent via WebSocket (same as text chat)
  8. Agent responds via text (streamed word-by-word as usual)
  9. Simultaneously: TTS converts response to audio, plays through speakers
  10. Agent's isometric character has a "speaking" animation with lip-sync approximation (mouth open/closed frames)

Hotword detection (optional, power feature):

  • "Hey Corner" or custom hotword set by client
  • Requires always-on mic permission (privacy concern, opt-in only)
  • Implementation: Picovoice (runs locally, no cloud, privacy-preserving) or Porcupine
  • If hotword detected: open chat bar, start recording. Same flow from step 2.

Visual integration:

  • Voice messages show a waveform in the chat (like iMessage voice messages)
  • Agent speech bubble in isometric view pulses when TTS is playing
  • Optional: subtitles overlay on the isometric view while agent speaks (accessibility, noisy environments)

Cost considerations:

  • ElevenLabs at $0.30/1k chars: average agent response is 200 chars = $0.06 per response
  • 50 voice responses/day per client = $3/day = $90/month per client
  • At $3-5k/month subscription, this is 2-3% of revenue. Acceptable.
  • Clients on Starter plan: Web Speech API only (free). Growth+: ElevenLabs voices available.

Privacy:

  • Voice data is NOT stored by default. STT converts to text, audio discarded.
  • Optional: "Save voice messages" toggle in Settings (stores audio in container volume, not Supabase)
  • Hotword detection runs locally (no cloud processing for wake word)
  • Clear privacy notice in Settings > Voice: "Your voice is converted to text and processed by your AI team. Audio is not stored unless you enable voice message history."

4. Corner SDK

Concept

Developers build entire applications on top of the Corner platform. Corner becomes infrastructure, not just a product. The SDK provides APIs for: agent management, task CRUD, real-time events, authentication, storage, and the isometric game engine.

Why This Matters

Every platform that became massive did it by letting others build on it: iOS (App Store), Shopify (apps), Slack (integrations), Salesforce (AppExchange). Corner's SDK turns every developer into a potential contributor to the ecosystem.

SDK use cases:

  • A CPA firm builds a custom tax deadline dashboard that reads from their Corner agents
  • A marketing agency builds a social media command center powered by Corner's content agents
  • A developer builds a time-tracking app that logs hours from Corner task completions
  • An analytics company builds a BI tool that pulls Corner data for cross-client benchmarks

SDK Components

1. REST API:

GET    /api/v1/agents                    # List agents
GET    /api/v1/agents/:id                # Agent detail
POST   /api/v1/agents/:id/message        # Send message to agent
GET    /api/v1/tasks                     # List tasks (filterable)
POST   /api/v1/tasks                     # Create task
PATCH  /api/v1/tasks/:id                 # Update task
GET    /api/v1/xp                        # XP summary
GET    /api/v1/reports/roi/:month        # ROI report data
GET    /api/v1/rooms                     # Room layouts
GET    /api/v1/skills                    # Installed skills

2. WebSocket API:

ws://api.corner.app/v1/stream
Events: agent_state_change, token_stream, task_complete, handoff, error_recovery

3. JavaScript SDK:

import { Corner } from '@corner/sdk';

const corner = new Corner({
  apiKey: 'ck_live_...',
  orgId: 'org_...'
});

// Send a message to an agent
const response = await corner.agents.message('operations', 'What are today\'s priorities?');

// Stream agent response
corner.stream.on('token', (token) => {
  console.log(token.agent, token.content);
});

// Create a task
await corner.tasks.create({
  agent: 'bobby',
  text: 'Build the pricing page',
  priority: 1
});

// Get ROI report
const roi = await corner.reports.roi('2026-03');
console.log(roi.hours_saved, roi.value_delivered);

4. Webhook API:

POST https://yourapp.com/corner-webhook
{
  "event": "task.completed",
  "agent": "operations",
  "task": { "id": "...", "text": "...", "completed_at": "..." },
  "org_id": "..."
}

API authentication:

  • API keys per organization (generated in Settings > Developer > API Keys)
  • Scoped permissions: read-only, read-write, admin
  • Rate limiting: 100 req/min for Starter, 500 for Growth, 2000 for Scale, custom for Enterprise
  • JWT for WebSocket (same as browser auth)

Developer portal (corner.app/developers):

  • API documentation (OpenAPI spec, interactive playground)
  • SDK downloads (npm package @corner/sdk)
  • Webhook configuration
  • API key management
  • Usage dashboard (requests, rate limit status)
  • Example apps and tutorials

Steffen design need: Developer portal design. API key management UI. Usage dashboard charts. Code snippet styling (syntax highlighting theme).

5. Enterprise Tier

Concept

Large organizations (50+ employees, compliance requirements, dedicated infrastructure needs) get a separate tier with features that SMBs don't need. This is the $10k+/month segment.

Enterprise Features

Single Sign-On (SSO):

  • SAML 2.0 and OIDC support
  • Integration with: Okta, Azure AD, Google Workspace, OneLogin
  • Provisioning: SCIM for automatic user creation/deactivation
  • Supabase Auth supports custom SAML providers

Service Level Agreement (SLA):

  • 99.9% uptime guarantee (43.8 min downtime/month allowed)
  • Response time SLA: <4 hours for critical, <24 hours for non-critical
  • Dedicated Slack channel for support (or in-app support agent)
  • Quarterly business reviews with AOM team

Dedicated Infrastructure:

  • Dedicated server (not shared with other clients)
  • Choice of region (US East, US West, EU, APAC)
  • Custom resource allocation (CPU, RAM, storage)
  • VPN peering for clients with on-premise systems
  • SOC 2 Type II compliance report (AOM maintains, client gets copy)

Advanced Security:

  • IP allowlisting for dashboard access
  • Audit log export (all user actions, agent actions, admin actions)
  • Data residency controls (data stays in specified region)
  • Encryption key management (client-managed keys via AWS KMS or similar)
  • Penetration test reports (annual, shared with client)

Custom Agents:

  • AOM builds custom agents specific to the enterprise's workflow
  • Dedicated agent development hours (20 hours/quarter included)
  • Priority access to new skills and features
  • Custom integration development (connect to client's internal systems)

Pricing:

  • Starting at $10,000/month
  • Custom based on: user count, agent count, infrastructure requirements, SLA level
  • Annual contracts with quarterly billing
  • Setup fee: $15-25k (includes custom agent development + integration)

Enterprise sales motion:

  • Not self-service. Requires AOM sales conversation.
  • "Contact Sales" CTA on pricing page > leads to calendar booking
  • Demo environment with sample enterprise data
  • POC (proof of concept): 30-day pilot at reduced rate

6. Third-Party Skill Marketplace

Concept

Other developers and consultants build skills for Corner. AOM reviews for quality and security, lists them in the gallery, handles billing, takes a revenue cut. This is Corner's "App Store" moment.

Implementation Notes

Developer program:

  • Sign up at corner.app/developers
  • Free to join. Build skills using the skill package format (from C5).
  • Submit skills via developer portal
  • AOM reviews within 5 business days
  • Approved skills listed in the gallery

Review process:

  • Automated: lint SKILL.md format, check skill-meta.json schema, run skill in sandbox container
  • Manual: AOM team reviews for quality, usefulness, security concerns
  • Rejection reasons: poor quality, duplicate of existing skill, security risk, inappropriate content
  • Appeal process: developer can revise and resubmit

Revenue share:

  • 70/30 split (developer 70%, AOM 30%)
  • AOM handles all billing (Stripe Connect for developer payouts)
  • Monthly payouts to developers (Stripe Connect payout schedule)
  • Minimum payout: $50 (accumulates if below threshold)
  • Developer dashboard: installs, revenue, ratings, reviews

Skill pricing models:

  • Free (developer donates, marketing for their consulting business)
  • Monthly subscription ($9.99-99.99/month per org that installs)
  • One-time purchase ($49-499)
  • Usage-based (rare, for API-heavy skills: $0.01-0.10 per execution)

Quality standards:

  • Must include: SKILL.md, skill-meta.json, README with description + screenshots
  • Must pass automated sandbox test (skill loads, responds to test triggers, doesn't crash)
  • Must not: access network without declaration, modify system files, exceed declared permissions
  • Must follow Corner UX guidelines (if skill has UI components)

Security model:

  • Skills run inside the client's container (same isolation as AOM skills)
  • Permission declarations in skill-meta.json: permissions: ["file_read", "file_write", "network"]
  • Client sees permissions before installing: "This skill can read and write files."
  • AOM code-reviews all network-accessing skills manually
  • Revocation: AOM can disable a skill across all containers (OTA kill switch)

7. API Integrations Marketplace

Concept

One-click integrations with the business tools clients already use. QuickBooks, Salesforce, HubSpot, Slack, Gmail, Zapier, Xero, FreshBooks, Monday.com, Asana.

Implementation Notes

How integrations work:

  • Integration = a skill + an OAuth connection
  • Client installs integration from the gallery > OAuth flow connects their account > skill syncs data
  • Example: "QuickBooks Integration" skill reads invoices from QuickBooks, triggers reminder agents when invoices are overdue

Priority integrations (by target vertical):

Integration Vertical What It Does
QuickBooks CPA, All Invoice sync, expense tracking, financial reporting agent
Xero CPA, All Same as QuickBooks, alternative accounting platform
Salesforce All Lead sync, deal pipeline, activity logging
HubSpot All Contact sync, email tracking, deal management
Slack All Notifications to Slack channels, two-way messaging
Gmail/Outlook All Email triage integration (beyond CC's built-in)
Zapier All Meta-integration (connect anything to Corner)
Procore Construction Project management, RFI tracking, submittal management
ServiceTitan Construction Dispatch, invoicing, customer management
Clio Law Case management, time tracking, billing
Practice Ignition CPA Client proposals, engagement letters

Zapier integration is the force multiplier. One Zapier integration = 5,000+ app connections. Corner trigger events (task_complete, agent_message, handoff) as Zapier triggers. Corner actions (create_task, send_message, update_status) as Zapier actions. This alone covers most integration needs without building individual connectors.

OAuth management:

  • Supabase integrations table (org_id, provider, access_token_encrypted, refresh_token_encrypted, scopes, connected_at)
  • Token encryption at rest (AES-256, key in environment variable)
  • Automatic token refresh before expiry
  • Settings > Integrations panel: connected apps with "Disconnect" option
  • OAuth callback: corner.app/api/integrations/callback/:provider

8. AI-to-AI Marketplace

Concept

Agents from different clients' offices collaborate on shared projects. A construction company's estimating agent works with a subcontractor's scheduling agent to bid a job together. Heavily permission-gated. This is the most ambitious C6 feature and may be C7.

Why This Is Radical

No AI product does this. Every AI tool is siloed to one user or one company. AI-to-AI collaboration across organizational boundaries is genuinely new. It's the "email between companies" moment for AI agents.

Implementation Notes (Very Early)

Permission model:

  • Both organizations must explicitly approve the collaboration
  • Data sharing scoped to the specific project (not full access)
  • Shared workspace: temporary container with limited context from both orgs
  • Audit log of all cross-org data exchanges
  • Either party can terminate collaboration instantly

Use cases:

  • General contractor's agent coordinates with subcontractor's agent on scheduling
  • CPA's agent requests documents from client's agent (the client also uses Corner)
  • Agency's content agent collaborates with brand's approval agent on campaign assets
  • Law firm's research agent shares findings with co-counsel's case agent

Technical sketch:

  • Shared project = new Supabase shared_projects record linking two org_ids
  • Shared workspace = temporary Docker container with read-only access to scoped data from both orgs
  • Communication: WebSocket bridge between the two org containers, mediated by the shared workspace
  • Data isolation: shared workspace cannot write to either org's container. It can only read designated files and produce output to the shared project space.
  • Output: both orgs get a copy of the shared project's deliverables

This needs more thinking. The security and privacy implications are significant. Cross-org data exposure, even scoped, is a compliance minefield. This feature needs a full security review before spec'ing.

Recommendation: build the API layer in C6 but don't ship the UI. Let power users (enterprise tier) pilot it manually. Full UI and self-service in C7.

9. Brand Furniture Partnerships

Concept

Real brands (Herman Miller, IKEA, Steelcase, Autonomous, FlexiSpot) pay AOM for furniture placement in the game. Their real products appear as purchasable items in the marketplace. "Product placement in a virtual office."

Why Brands Would Pay

  • Targeted audience: business owners and decision-makers who actually buy office furniture
  • High engagement: clients interact with their office daily (C5 XP/streaks ensure this)
  • Purchase intent: if someone puts a Herman Miller Aeron in their virtual office, they're thinking about the real one
  • Attribution: "Buy the real one" link from the virtual item to the brand's store (affiliate revenue)

Revenue Model

  • Placement fee: Brand pays AOM $5-20k/year for their product line in the game
  • Affiliate commission: 5-10% on real purchases driven by Corner (tracked via affiliate links)
  • Exclusive packs: Brand sponsors a limited-edition pack ($0 to client, brand pays AOM for distribution)
  • Data insights (anonymized): Which items are most placed, engagement metrics, demographic breakdown of users who place brand items. Never PII. Aggregated only.

Implementation

  • Furniture catalog: brand_id field on items. Brand items marked with brand logo badge.
  • "Real Product" badge on brand items with link to purchase page
  • Brand dashboard: brands see placement counts, click-through rates, purchase attributions
  • Contract management: legal agreement per brand (Patrik/Ash handles)

This requires business development, not engineering. The C5 furniture marketplace is the platform. C6 adds the brand partnership layer on top.

C6 Priorities (Rough Order)

Priority Feature Why First
1 White-label Multiplies sales capacity without AOM effort. Revenue impact is immediate.
2 Enterprise tier $10k+/month clients. High revenue per client. Requires SSO + SLA + dedicated infra.
3 Third-party skills Ecosystem play. More skills = more value = more retention. Developer community.
4 Multi-language Spanish first (Phoenix market). Opens international expansion.
5 API integrations QuickBooks/Salesforce/Zapier. Clients expect integrations.
6 Corner SDK Developer platform. Enables everything else (third-party skills use SDK).
7 Voice interface Differentiator. "Talk to your AI team." Wow factor in demos.
8 Brand partnerships Revenue, but requires biz dev. Lower priority than platform features.
9 AI-to-AI marketplace Most ambitious. Needs full security review. Possibly C7.

C7 Horizon (Very Early Thinking)

Not even notes yet. Just one-liners captured.

  • Corner Academy: courses on AI operations, built into the platform. Clients level up their knowledge, not just their agents.
  • Video agents (Cleo evolution): agents that see via camera (webcam, screen share) and produce video. Visual QA, screen recording analysis, video content generation.
  • Predictive agents: agents that anticipate needs before the client asks. "I noticed your Q1 numbers are behind. Here's a plan to close the gap." Proactive, not reactive.
  • Corner for Teams: multi-user collaboration in one office. Different team members chat with different agents simultaneously. Shared task board. Team XP.
  • Industry-specific Corner editions: Corner for Construction, Corner for Law, Corner for Healthcare. Pre-configured agents, skills, and onboarding tailored to each vertical. Separate marketing, same platform.
  • Offline mode (full): run Corner locally when internet is down. Sync when reconnected. For field workers.
  • Corner Marketplace for data: anonymized, aggregated insights across the platform. "Businesses like yours typically complete 45 tasks/month in their first quarter." Benchmark data.

C6 is where Corner stops being AOM's product and becomes an ecosystem that runs without AOM in the room. Resellers sell it, developers build for it, enterprise clients depend on it, and brands want placement in it. That's the inflection point: when the platform grows faster than the company that built it.

"A million worlds. And everyone's building one."
